title.value: JASMINE: Scale up JavaScript Static Security Analysis with Computation-based Semantic Explanation
JASMINE: Scale up JavaScript Static Security Analysis with Computation-based Semantic Explanation

abstract.value: Static data flow analysis techniques have been broadly applied in analyzing and detecting security threats in web applications. However, without actual code execution, they often suffer serious precision issues and may even miss serious vulnerabilities, especially when facing modern JavaScript applications characterized by complex operations and semantics. To combat these complex semantics, we propose a novel semantic understanding approach, namely computation-based semantic explanation (CSE). CSE can effectively identify and resolve common failures arising from complex semantics in static data flow analysis, ultimately improving the detection of potential vulnerabilities. We implement a prototype tool of CSE, called JASMINE. By applying JASMINE to more than 10K real-world JavaScript programs, we find complex operations and semantics are prevalent in practice and heavily impede the state-of-art static techniques (e.g., Github's CodeQL and IBM's WALA) from regular security validations. Our experiments show JASMINE can effectively resolve complex semantics and lead to the discovery of 22 hidden vulnerabilities, which are not detectable by existing tools. Among these vulnerabilities, 13 ones are previously unknown, i.e., zero-day vulnerabilities. Up to now, nine CVEs have been issued, and five of them have been rated as 'critical' with a 9.8 severity score. 296 2024 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

Static data flow analysis techniques have been broadly applied in analyzing and detecting security threats in web applications. However, without actual code execution, they often suffer serious precision issues and may even miss serious vulnerabilities, especially when facing modern JavaScript ap- plications characterized by complex operations and semantics. To combat these complex semantics, we propose a novel semantic understanding approach, namely computation-based semantic explanation (CSE). CSE can effectively identify and resolve common failures arising from complex semantics in static data flow analysis, ultimately improving the detection of potential vulnerabilities. We implement a prototype tool of CSE, called J ASMINE . By applying J ASMINE to more than 10K real-world JavaScript programs, we find complex operations and semantics are prevalent in practice and heavily impede the state-of-art static techniques (e.g., Github's CodeQL and IBM's W ALA) from regular security validations. Our experiments show J ASMINE can effectively resolve complex semantics and lead to the discovery of 22 hidden vulnerabilities, which are not detectable by existing tools. Among these vulnerabilities, 13 ones are previously unknown, i.e., zero-day vulnerabilities. Up to now, nine CVEs have been issued, and five of them have been rated as ‘critical' with a 9.8 severity score. 1. Introduction JavaScript has been widely utilized for various pro- gram development with the rise of Node.js package man- ager (npm) supply-chain platform. For example, many pop- ular desktop applications such as Microsoft Teams and Slack [21], [23] are developed in JavaScript. With the rapid growth of the ecosystem, cybercriminals have set npm as their primary target, launching multiple attacks such as supply-chain code poisoning [29]. Furthermore, like other web applications, JavaScript programs suffer various secu- rity vulnerabilities, such as remote code execution and injec- tion vulnerabilities [47], [55], [46], [44], [56]. Due to npm's highly transitive and dependent nature, a new vulnerability can quickly affect numerous programs. Therefore, there is a need for efficient and scalable security checks that can handle a large number of JavaScript packages and their frequent updates. Static program analysis techniques have great potential for validating npm security due to their highly scalable nature. One such technique, static data flow analysis, has proven to be especially useful for various downstream se- curity validation tasks like taint tracking and type inconsis- tency detection. This technique has contributed significantly to the detection of numerous critical JavaScript vulnera- bilities. However, despite their success, conventional static data flow analysis approaches face critical challenges and hardly scale to modern JavaScript applications. One im- portant and well-known problem is the complex semantics [27] in JavaScript. Due to JavaScript's intrinsic flexibility and dynamic stretching, JavaScript programs have extensive and diverse complex operations and semantic units, such as dynamic properties and first-class functions. These complex semantics raise analysis challenges for regular data flow analysis and even cause analysis failures and false detection negatives, i.e., failing to hunt vulnerabilities hidden in the deep. Recently, several techniques [27], [26], [2], [45] were proposed to mitigate the complex JavaScript semantic issues, but they have shortcomings in scalability and accuracy. They usually rely on a modeling-based analysis strategy that summarizes how a semantic unit should be interpreted through a set of rules. For example, Sridharan et al. [45] pro- posed heuristics-based taint propagation rules for dynamic property access semantics in JavaScript. However, these modeling-based approaches are labor-intensive and cannot cover all sub-situations, and the manually defined rules are difficult to maintain and update. Worse still, JavaScript is rapidly evolving. In recent three years, over 40 new syntax and language features have been introduced [13]. Taking ac- count of the fast-evolving situation, prior approaches hardly scale to the changes. In practice, state-of-the-art tools often have to ignore these semantics for avoiding analysis errors, inevitably causing false negatives. In this paper, we present a new method, i.e., computation-based semantic explanation (CSE) , to mitigate the complex semantic problem. In contrast to conventional modeling-based approaches, CSE adapts a novel computa- tional method that can resolve complex semantics in a scal- able and automatic way. First, CSE simplifies the compli- cated relationships between regular static data flow analysis and complex semantics into a single semantic model. This allows for a consistent detection method of various complex 296 DOI 10.1109/SP54263.2024.00183 semantics and operations. Second, CSE understands these instructions by extracting them into a minimal executable unit and using dynamic analysis to determine their actual behaviors. Finally, CSE addresses the complex semantics by encoding the observed behaviors into the target program using source-to-source transformation. This approach allows existing analysis tools to easily comprehend complex seman- tics by analyzing the transformed code. As a result, CSE can be integrated into various analysis tools (e.g., serving as a front-end preprocessor for targeted programs). We implemented our CSE method in a prototype system called J ASMINE (JAvascript SeMantic INtErpretation). By using JASMINE on real-world npm packages, we found that complex semantics are prevalent and significantly impact static security analysis tools. In particular, J ASMINE identi- fied 28,016 analysis failures due to complex semantics. We demonstrated that J ASMINE is capable of resolving analysis failures. Specifically, out of the identified failures, J ASMINE was able to conduct analysis on 18,181 of them and un- covered more than 90,000 program states. As a result, J AS- MINE discovered 22 “hidden” vulnerabilities, including 13 zero-day vulnerabilities, which were mostly undetectable by existing tools. 12 CVEs have been issued, with five rated as critical and disclosed with a 9.8 severity score. Additionally, our study confirms that JASMINE can enhance existing static security tools by increasing vulnerability detection rates and improving analysis coverage (often doubling the number of discovered taint paths). The implementation of J ASMINE will be open-sourced to help with research on complex se- mantics in JavaScript https://github.com/xiaofen9/Jasmine. In summary, we make the following three major contri- butions in the paper. • A new approach. We propose CSE, a novel approach to mitigate the daunting complex semantic problem. In contrast to existing modeling-based methods, CSE takes a computation-based approach to reason and sim- plify semantics uniformly. • A new tool. We implement a new tool, called JASMINE , to apply the CSE approach to npm programs. It can automatically identify and resolve complex semantics in seconds, and can be integrated with many existing static tools to enhance their effectiveness. • Extensive evaluation with hard-to-detect security vulnerabilities. We apply J ASMINE to over 10,000 npm programs, leading to the discovery of 28,000+ semantic blockers. We find J ASMINE can dramatically improve state-of-the-art static security analysis tools such as CodeQL. It identified 22 hidden vulnerabilities, resulting in vendors assigning 12 CVEs. Of the 5 publicly disclosed CVEs, all had a severity score of 9.8, and were classified as "critical." 2. Background on Analysis Challenges This section first briefly discusses our target problem and assumptions (§2.1). Then, it walks through a concrete example of how complex semantics causes failures in real- world vulnerability detection (§2.2). 2.1. Problem Statement Problem Scope. Static program analysis techniques have been widely utilized in detecting web application vulner- abilities. But the state-of-the-art tools struggle to analyze complex language semantics, leading to security validation failures. The npm ecosystem presents several popular cases of such complex semantics and operations (we will discuss concrete examples of these semantics in the next section). • Flexible or advanced built-in syntax (e.g., ES6 syntax). • Operations with dynamic properties. • Third-party API usages. • First-class functions (e.g., callback). In particular, static data flow analysis, one of the most widely used security program analysis techniques, is severely impacted by the above complex semantics. Precise tracking of how data is processed in the target program is crucial for static data flow analysis, but the complex seman- tics make this difficult. For instance, a callback function can be called from various parts of a program, making it challenging to identify the origin of specific data. In this paper, we focus on dealing with analysis failures during static data flow analysis Threat Model and Assumptions. Our threat model targets benign but vulnerable npm programs. Based on our scope definition above, our goal is to assist security tools that use static data flow analysis to detect vulnerabilities obscured by complex semantics. However, it is important to note that our approach may not provide complete accuracy in analyzing complex semantics (please see detailed discussion in §10). Consequently, our approach is more appropriate for aiding practical security tools such as CodeQL and W ALA, which do not require absolute soundness or completeness. 2.2. Real-World Example In this section, we walk through a real-world vulnera- bility CVE-2019-10781 [6] of an npm package. We demon- strate how existing tools fail to conduct regular static data flow analysis and eventually miss this vulnerability. For convenience, in the following content of this paper, we use T as shorthand for static data flow analysis-based security tools that satisfy our assumptions in §2.1. The vulnerability is found from a widely-used input validation npm package ‘schema-inspector' (28K+ monthly downloads), which provides the functionality of sanitizing sensitive input for Node.js applications. The vulnerability got a ‘9.8' CVSS score (out of 10) and was rated as ‘critical'. Figure 1 shows the simplified vulnerable code. The left-most code box shows how the package accepts external input and conducts security validation. The box in the middle shows the vulnerable logic, which locates at Line 21. The right-most code box shows the package's initialization logic, where the package's complex semantics and operations locate. The vulnerability is caused by a risky data flow from the external input data at Line 5 to function validate_string() at Line 20, shown by the grey lines. 297
